title: Transaction Fundamentals: BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK
description: Understand ACID guarantees, explicit transactions, savepoints, and multi-statement atomicity.

data.text: A **Transaction** bundles multiple SQL statements into a single all-or-nothing unit of work. PostgreSQL enforces ACID properties: Atomicity (all succeed or none do), Consistency (constraints are never violated), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere), and Durability (committed data survives crashes).

data.title: Atomic Financial Balance Transfer with Savepoint
data.content: Using SAVEPOINT to roll back a nested step without aborting the entire transaction.

data.text: A savepoint marks a point you can roll back to without discarding the whole transaction. This matters because a single failed statement normally aborts the entire transaction: after an error, every subsequent statement is rejected with `current transaction is aborted` until you either `ROLLBACK` or `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT`.

data.title: Recover from a failed step and continue
data.content: The second insert violates a constraint; rolling back to the savepoint restores the transaction to a usable state so the third insert still succeeds.

data.title: Interview angle: transactions and connection state
data.text: A transaction is bound to a connection, so pooling tools must return connections in a clean state. An application that leaves a transaction open after an exception poisons that connection for the next request. That is why connection poolers run a reset query, and why frameworks wrap each request in a transaction that is always committed or rolled back in a `finally` block. Being able to connect transactions, connection pooling, and error handling is a strong answer.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` to ensure atomic multi-step operations.
Use `SAVEPOINT` to handle partial rollbacks within a transaction.
